stem: Which document states the results required and how performance will be measured, leaving the method to the contractor?

options.text: Performance work statement (PWS)
options.why: A PWS describes outcomes and measurable standards: the core of performance-based acquisition.

options.text: Statement of work (SOW)
options.why: A SOW often prescribes how the work is done.

options.text: Statement of objectives (SOO)
options.why: A SOO states only goals; offerors write the PWS.

options.text: Independent Government cost estimate (IGCE)
options.why: The IGCE is a cost estimate, not a requirement document.

stem: When the Government issues a statement of objectives (SOO), offerors are expected to:

options.text: Propose their own performance work statement to meet the objectives
options.why: The SOO gives the goals; each offeror proposes how it will meet them in a PWS.

options.text: Price the Government's detailed step-by-step instructions
options.why: A SOO deliberately leaves out detailed instructions.

options.text: Submit only a price, since the SOO already defines every task
options.why: A SOO needs a proposed approach from the offeror.

options.text: Write the Government's quality assurance surveillance plan for approval
options.why: The QASP is the Government's plan.

stem: What is a quality assurance surveillance plan (QASP)?

options.text: The Government's plan for checking the contractor's work
options.why: It says what will be checked, how and how often.

options.text: The contractor's internal quality control plan
options.why: That is the contractor's quality control plan, not the Government's QASP.

options.text: The pricing schedule for the services and the payment terms
options.why: Prices are in the schedule, not the QASP.

options.text: The source selection plan for evaluating the offers
options.why: The source selection plan governs evaluation before award.

stem: Which arrangement is a prohibited personal services contract (unless a statute authorizes it)?

options.text: Contractor staff working under relatively continuous supervision by Government employees
options.why: Government supervision of contractor staff creates the employer-employee relationship that defines personal services.

options.text: A help desk run by the contractor's own supervisors and measured by response times
options.why: The contractor manages its people; the Government judges results.

options.text: A grounds maintenance contract with performance standards
options.why: That is a normal performance-based service contract.

options.text: A firm-fixed-price training course that the contractor designs and delivers to Government staff
options.why: Delivering a defined service at a fixed price is not personal services.

stem: Which function is inherently governmental and may not be contracted out?

options.text: Awarding contracts on behalf of the Government
options.why: Binding the Government is reserved for Government officials.

options.text: Mowing grass and trimming trees on the installation
options.why: Grounds maintenance is a commercial service.

options.text: Running an IT help desk
options.why: Help desk support is commonly contracted.

options.text: Drafting training slides for Government review
options.why: Support work reviewed and approved by the Government can be contracted.

stem: When does the FAR require market research?

options.text: Before writing new requirements and before soliciting above the SAT
options.why: Those are the two points FAR 10.001 names.

options.text: Only for buys over $10 million, where a formal market research report is needed
options.why: Market research is required well below that.

options.text: Only for sole-source buys, to prove no one else can do the work
options.why: Market research supports every strategy, competitive or not.

options.text: Only after award, to confirm the price was fair and reasonable
options.why: Market research comes before solicitation.

stem: A notice asking industry who can meet a need, before the Government decides how to buy, is a:

options.text: Sources sought notice or request for information
options.why: They gather market information for planning. Responses are not offers, and the FAR leaves the research method to you (10.001(c), 15.101(c)).

options.text: Presolicitation notice for a planned buy
options.why: A presolicitation notice announces a planned solicitation.

options.text: Award synopsis on SAM.gov
options.why: An award synopsis announces an award already made.

options.text: Solicitation amendment asking for capability statements
options.why: An amendment changes a solicitation that has been issued.

stem: How much documentation does market research need?

options.text: Enough to match the size and complexity of the acquisition
options.why: The FAR scales documentation to the buy.

options.text: None, unless a vendor protests the acquisition strategy
options.why: Results must be documented as part of the file.

options.text: A 20-page report for every buy over the micro-purchase threshold
options.why: The FAR does not require a fixed length.

options.text: Only what the contractors provide in their capability statements
options.why: The Government documents its own research.

stem: Market research should look first for:

options.text: Commercial products and commercial services
options.why: The FAR puts commercial solutions first.

options.text: The incumbent contractor and its current prices
options.why: Market research looks at the whole market, not just the incumbent.

options.text: Custom-developed solutions built to Government specifications
options.why: Custom solutions come only when commercial ones will not work.

options.text: Foreign sources with lower labor costs
options.why: Domestic preference laws often apply; foreign sources are not the starting point.

stem: During market research, what may you share with industry?

options.text: The same general information for everyone, such as a draft requirement
options.why: Early exchanges are encouraged when every interested firm gets the same information.

options.text: The independent Government cost estimate, so prices come in realistic
options.why: The IGCE is protected Government information.

options.text: The incumbent's current prices and its staffing levels
options.why: That would release one firm's information to its competitors.

options.text: One vendor's technical approach, to help the others understand the need
options.why: That discloses proprietary information.

stem: When must you buy a supply item from Federal Prison Industries (FPI)?

options.text: When FPI makes it and FPI's product is comparable in price, quality and delivery
options.why: FPI is a required source only when its product is comparable.

options.text: Always, whatever the price or delivery time, because FPI is a mandatory source
options.why: FPI has no blanket priority regardless of comparability.

options.text: Never; DoW buyers are exempt from the FPI rules by statute
options.why: DoW buyers apply the FPI rules.

options.text: Only for overseas requirements, where commercial U.S. vendors cannot deliver in time
options.why: The FPI rules are not limited to overseas buys.

stem: Products and services on the AbilityOne Procurement List must be bought from:

options.text: AbilityOne participating nonprofit agencies
options.why: AbilityOne is a mandatory source for listed items.

options.text: Any small business
options.why: AbilityOne listing makes the nonprofit agencies the required source.

options.text: The lowest-priced commercial vendor
options.why: Listed items are not competed on the open market.

options.text: GSA schedule holders only, through GSA Advantage
options.why: The schedules are not the required source for AbilityOne items.

stem: Before buying on the open market, what should you check first?

options.text: Required sources and existing contracts
options.why: FAR Part 8 sets that order of precedence.

options.text: Only GSA Advantage, for the lowest price
options.why: GSA is one place to look, but required sources come first.

options.text: Whether GAO has a pending protest
options.why: That is not part of source selection precedence.

options.text: The incumbent's availability
options.why: Incumbents get no special status.

stem: What is the title of FAR Part 8?

options.text: Required Sources of Supplies and Services
options.why: Part 8 covers mandatory sources and the Federal Supply Schedules.

options.text: Acquisition Planning
options.why: That is Part 7.

options.text: Acquisition of Commercial Products and Commercial Services
options.why: That is Part 12.

options.text: Describing Agency Needs
options.why: That is Part 11.

stem: After the FAR Overhaul, which FAR part covers the GSA Federal Supply Schedules?

options.text: Part 8 (Subpart 8.4)
options.why: Part 38 was removed; the schedule coverage now sits in Subpart 8.4, with ordering procedures in GSA's regulation.

options.text: Part 38 (Federal Supply Schedule Contracting)
options.why: Part 38 is reserved after the overhaul.

options.text: Part 13 (Subpart 13.3)
options.why: Part 13 covers noncommercial simplified procedures.

options.text: Part 15 (Subpart 15.4)
options.why: Part 15 covers contracting by negotiation.

stem: Under the rule of two, a contract above the micro-purchase threshold must be set aside for small business when you reasonably expect offers from:

options.text: Two or more responsible small businesses at fair market prices
options.why: That is the rule of two in RFO FAR 19.104-1(a).

options.text: At least one responsible small business at a fair market price
options.why: One small business is not enough for a total set-aside.

options.text: Three or more small businesses in the local area
options.why: The rule is two, and location is not the test.

options.text: Any 8(a) firm or HUBZone small business
options.why: 8(a) awards follow their own rules; the rule of two is about small businesses generally.

stem: Who sets the size standards that decide whether a business is small?

options.text: The Small Business Administration, by NAICS code
options.why: SBA size standards are tied to the NAICS code the contracting officer picks.

options.text: The contracting officer, based on the contract's value
options.why: The contracting officer picks the NAICS code; SBA sets the standard.

options.text: DCAA
options.why: DCAA audits; it does not set size standards.

options.text: The offeror
options.why: Offerors certify their size against SBA's standard.

stem: You decide not to set aside a $500,000 buy for small business. What must you do?

options.text: Document the reason in the file
options.why: RFO FAR 19.104-1(b)(1) requires documenting why a contract is not set aside.

options.text: Get GAO approval
options.why: GAO does not approve set-aside decisions.

options.text: Post a justification for other than full and open competition
options.why: Not setting aside means full and open competition; no J&A is needed.

options.text: Nothing; the decision is the contracting officer's alone
options.why: It is the contracting officer's decision, but it must be documented.

stem: HUBZone, SDVOSB, WOSB and 8(a) are:

options.text: Small business programs in FAR Part 19
options.why: Each is a socioeconomic small business program with its own set-aside and sole-source rules.

options.text: Required sources under FAR Part 8
options.why: Part 8 required sources are things like AbilityOne and FPI.

options.text: Contract types for small business buys
options.why: Contract types are in Part 16.

options.text: Protest forums for small business issues
options.why: Protests go to the agency, GAO or the Court of Federal Claims.

stem: Does FAR Part 19 require small business set-asides for contracts awarded and performed overseas?

options.text: No. It applies in the U.S. and outlying areas; agencies may apply it elsewhere
options.why: FAR 19.000(b) makes Part 19 optional outside the U.S. and its outlying areas.

options.text: Yes, Part 19 applies everywhere a U.S. agency awards and performs a contract
options.why: Part 19 states a geographic scope.

options.text: No, Part 19 may never be used overseas because host-nation agreements forbid it
options.why: Agencies may choose to apply it outside the U.S.

options.text: Only for construction, where local firms must get set-asides
options.why: The scope rule is not tied to construction.

stem: A total small business set-aside is:

options.text: Full and open competition after excluding sources
options.why: Set-asides exclude large firms but keep competition open to all eligible small businesses.

options.text: Other than full and open competition
options.why: Set-asides are not one of the seven exceptions.

options.text: A sole-source award
options.why: Several small businesses compete.

options.text: Something that requires a justification and approval
options.why: No J&A is needed for a set-aside.

stem: Which RFO FAR section is the 'only one responsible source' exception?

options.why: The old 6.302-1 is now 6.103-1.
6.103-2 is unusual and compelling urgency.
6.103-5 is authorized or required by statute.
6.104 covers the justification and approval itself.

stem: For DoW, who approves a $50 million justification for other than full and open competition?

options.text: The competition advocate
options.why: DFARS 206.104-71 Table 206-1: over $10 million up to $100 million goes to the competition advocate.

options.text: The contracting officer
options.why: The contracting officer's level in DoW is $10 million or below.

options.text: The head of the contracting activity
options.why: The HCA tier in DoW starts above $100 million.

options.text: The senior procurement executive
options.why: The SPE tier in DoW is above $500 million.

stem: For DoW, who approves an $8 million sole-source justification?

options.text: The contracting officer, by certifying the justification
options.why: In DoW's Table 206-1, $10 million or below is the contracting officer's level.

options.text: The competition advocate for the contracting activity
options.why: That tier starts above $10 million in DoW.

options.text: The head of the contracting activity (HCA)
options.why: That tier starts above $100 million in DoW.

options.text: The senior procurement executive (SPE)
options.why: That tier is above $500 million.

stem: Which is NOT one of the seven exceptions to full and open competition?

options.text: The customer prefers the incumbent
options.why: Preference is not a statutory exception.

options.text: Unusual and compelling urgency
options.why: That is 6.103-2.

options.text: National security
options.why: That is 6.103-6.

options.text: International agreement
options.why: That is 6.103-4.

stem: Who prepares the independent Government cost estimate (IGCE)?

options.text: The Government (usually the customer), without using offerors' numbers
options.why: Independence is the point of the IGCE.

options.text: The incumbent contractor, since it knows the real costs of doing the work today
options.why: A contractor-prepared estimate is not independent.

options.text: Each offeror, with its proposal, so the estimates can be compared
options.why: Offerors submit prices, not the Government's estimate.

options.text: DCAA, after auditing the likely offerors' rates
options.why: DCAA audits contractor costs; it does not prepare IGCEs.

stem: May you share the IGCE with offerors?

options.text: No
options.why: The IGCE is protected Government information; sharing it would skew offers.

options.text: Yes, after the solicitation closes
options.why: It stays protected through award.

options.text: Yes, if an offeror asks in writing
options.why: A written request does not make release proper.

options.text: Yes, but only with small businesses
options.why: Sharing with some offerors would also be unfair.

stem: When should acquisition planning begin?

options.text: As soon as the need is identified
options.why: Early planning gives time for research, documents and reviews.

options.text: After the funds are about to expire
options.why: That is too late and invites fiscal mistakes.

options.text: Only after the solicitation is written
options.why: Planning shapes the solicitation.

options.text: After award
options.why: Planning comes first.

stem: Consolidating or bundling requirements in a way likely to keep small businesses out requires:

options.text: Market research and a written determination
options.why: RFO FAR 7.107-2 requires both before consolidating or bundling.

options.text: Nothing, if it saves money for the Government
options.why: Savings must be shown and documented.

options.text: GAO approval before the solicitation
options.why: GAO does not pre-approve bundling.

options.text: The incumbent's consent
options.why: The incumbent has no approval role.

stem: What is the title of FAR Part 7?

options.text: Acquisition Planning
options.why: Part 7 covers acquisition plans, bundling and inherently governmental functions.

options.text: Market Research
options.why: That is Part 10.

options.text: Competition Requirements
options.why: That is Part 6.

options.text: Types of Contracts
options.why: That is Part 16.

stem: Which contract type puts the most cost risk on the contractor?

options.text: Firm-fixed-price
options.why: The price does not change with the contractor's actual costs.

options.text: Cost-plus-fixed-fee
options.why: The Government reimburses allowable costs.

options.text: Time-and-materials
options.why: The Government pays for the hours used.

options.text: Cost-plus-award-fee
options.why: Costs are reimbursed; only the fee is at risk.

stem: A cost-reimbursement contract may be used only when:

options.text: Fixed price is not workable, the contractor's accounting is adequate, and the Government can monitor costs
options.why: Those conditions protect the Government when it carries the cost risk.

options.text: The contractor prefers it, has a cost accounting system, and offers a lower fee
options.why: Contract type is the Government's decision based on risk.

options.text: The item is commercial, the price is very uncertain, and the customer agrees in writing to share the cost risk
options.why: Commercial buys use fixed-price types.

options.text: The value is below the SAT, funds are available, and the COR can monitor costs
options.why: Dollar value alone does not justify cost-type.

stem: Which contract types are used for commercial products and services?

options.text: Firm-fixed-price or fixed-price with economic price adjustment
options.why: RFO FAR 12.104 prefers these for commercial buys; T&M and labor-hour need a determination.

options.text: Cost-plus-fixed-fee or cost-plus-incentive-fee, for flexibility
options.why: Cost-type contracts are not used for commercial items.

options.text: Cost-plus-award-fee, to reward commercial best practices
options.why: Cost-type contracts are not used for commercial items.

options.text: Letter contracts only, definitized within 180 days
options.why: Letter contracts are a rare stopgap, not the commercial norm.

stem: Which contract type is least preferred because it gives the contractor no profit incentive to control costs or labor?

options.text: Time-and-materials
options.why: Paying by the hour rewards more hours, so T&M needs a ceiling and close surveillance.

options.text: Firm-fixed-price
options.why: FFP gives the strongest incentive to control cost.

options.text: Fixed-price incentive
options.why: Its share ratio rewards cost control.

options.text: Indefinite-delivery indefinite-quantity
options.why: IDIQ describes delivery terms, not cost incentive; its orders can be fixed price.

stem: An indefinite-delivery indefinite-quantity (IDIQ) contract:

options.text: States a minimum and maximum, with orders placed as needs arise
options.why: The guaranteed minimum makes it binding; orders fill actual needs.

options.text: Buys a fixed quantity delivered all at once on a set date
options.why: That is a definite quantity, single delivery.

options.text: Needs no minimum quantity because orders are optional
options.why: A minimum is required for consideration.

options.text: Allows only one order, placed at the time of award
options.why: IDIQs exist to allow many orders.

stem: What is the standard micro-purchase threshold in October 2026?

options.why: Raised from $10,000 by the inflation adjustment effective 1 October 2025.
That was the threshold before 1 October 2025.
That was the threshold years ago.
That applies to qualifying contingency or emergency buys inside the U.S.

stem: What is the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) in October 2026?

options.why: Raised from $250,000 effective 1 October 2025.
That was the SAT before 1 October 2025.
That was the SAT before 2018.
That is a contingency SAT inside the U.S.

stem: Under the RFO FAR, up to what amount may simplified procedures be used for commercial products and services (no contingency)?

options.text: $9 million
options.why: RFO FAR 12.201-1 allows simplified procedures for commercial buys up to $9 million.

options.text: $7.5 million
options.why: That was the ceiling before the 2025 inflation adjustment.
That is the SAT, which is lower.

options.text: $15 million
options.why: $15 million applies only with a contingency or emergency determination.

stem: Under the RFO FAR, Part 13 simplified procedures apply to:

options.text: Noncommercial products and services at or below the SAT
options.why: Commercial simplified buys moved to Part 12; Part 13 kept noncommercial ones.

options.text: All buys under the SAT, commercial or not
options.why: Commercial buys now follow Part 12.

options.text: Commercial products and services up to $9 million in value
options.why: That is Part 12.

options.text: Micro-purchases only, with the purchase card
options.why: Micro-purchases follow Subpart 12.4.

stem: In sealed bidding, award goes to:

options.text: The responsible, responsive bidder whose bid is lowest on price and price-related factors
options.why: Sealed bidding is decided on price, with no discussions.

options.text: The best value after a technical tradeoff between price and past performance
options.why: Tradeoffs belong to negotiated buys.

options.text: The highest technically rated bidder, if its price is reasonable
options.why: Technical ratings are not used in sealed bidding.

options.text: The incumbent, if its price is within 10% of the lowest bid
options.why: There is no incumbent preference.

stem: A customer asks you to split a $40,000 requirement into three purchase card buys. What is the rule?

options.text: Splitting a requirement to fit under a threshold is prohibited
options.why: Requirements may not be divided to avoid thresholds or procedures.

options.text: It is fine if each buy is under the micro-purchase threshold
options.why: Staying under the threshold by splitting is exactly what is prohibited.

options.text: It is fine if different cardholders make the buys
options.why: Using several cardholders is still splitting.

options.text: It is fine at year-end, when funds would otherwise expire
options.why: There is no year-end exception.

stem: Which clause holds the standard terms and conditions for commercial products and services?

options.why: 52.212-4, Contract Terms and Conditions: Commercial Products and Commercial Services.
52.212-1 is the instructions to offerors.
52.212-2 is the evaluation provision.
52.243-1 is the Changes clause for fixed-price contracts.

stem: What is a combined synopsis/solicitation?

options.text: One notice that is both the synopsis and the solicitation for a commercial buy
options.why: It saves time by combining the two.

options.text: A solicitation that covers two different contracts, with one closing date for both
options.why: It is one buy with one notice.

options.text: The posting of a sole-source justification with the synopsis
options.why: Justifications are posted separately.

options.text: An award announcement combined with the debriefing notice
options.why: Award notices come after award.

stem: For a commercial item, certified cost or pricing data are:

options.text: Not required: commercial items are an exception
options.why: Commercial products and services are one of the listed exceptions.

options.text: Always required above $2.5 million
options.why: The commercial exception applies at any value.

options.text: Required for services only
options.why: The exception covers commercial products and services.

options.text: Required whenever the contracting officer wants them
options.why: When an exception applies, certified data may not be required.

stem: How are commercial contracts terminated?

options.text: Under the commercial clause (52.212-4), for convenience or cause, not under Part 49
options.why: RFO FAR 12.304 keeps commercial terminations under the commercial terms.

options.text: Only for default, after a cure notice and a show cause notice
options.why: Commercial contracts can also be terminated for convenience.

options.text: Only under the FAR Part 49 settlement procedures and forms, the same as any other contract
options.why: Part 49 may guide but does not govern commercial terminations.

options.text: They cannot be terminated once the commercial item is delivered
options.why: The commercial clause allows termination.

stem: When may you limit a commercial buy to one brand?

options.text: Only with the justification FAR Part 6 requires
options.why: RFO FAR 12.102 forbids restricting competition without the required justification and approval.

options.text: Whenever the customer prefers the brand and pays for it
options.why: Preference alone does not justify restricting competition.

options.text: Always below the SAT, with no documentation
options.why: Below the SAT you still document why only one source is available.

options.text: Never, even with a justification
options.why: It is allowed when properly justified.

stem: Under the RFO FAR, a presolicitation notice is required for proposed actions expected to exceed:

options.text: $20,000, unless an exemption applies
options.why: RFO FAR 5.101(a) uses $20,000.

options.text: $25,000, unless the buy is commercial
options.why: $25,000 is where the 15-day advance notice applies; the notice itself starts above $20,000.

options.text: $15,000, the micro-purchase threshold
options.why: $15,000 is the micro-purchase threshold.

options.text: $350,000, the simplified acquisition threshold
options.why: That is the SAT.

stem: For a noncommercial action above $25,000, how far ahead of the solicitation must the notice be published?

options.text: At least 15 days
options.why: RFO FAR 5 Table 5-2 sets 15 days above $25,000.

options.text: At least 10 days
options.why: Ten days applies to the $20,000 to $25,000 band.

options.text: At least 30 days
options.why: Thirty days is a response time, not the notice lead time.

options.text: At least 45 days
options.why: Forty-five days is the R&D response time.

stem: For most noncommercial buys not covered by other rules, how long must offerors have to respond?

options.text: At least 30 days after the solicitation is issued
options.why: Thirty days is the general minimum for those buys.

options.text: At least 15 days after the notice is published
options.why: Fifteen days is the notice lead time, not the response time.

options.text: At least 45 days after the solicitation is issued
options.why: Forty-five days applies to research and development.

options.text: No minimum, if the contracting officer finds the time reasonable
options.why: Only at or below the SAT and for commercial buys is it 'a reasonable time'.

stem: In a uniform contract format solicitation, which pair is correct?

options.text: Instructions say what to submit; evaluation factors say how offers will be judged
options.why: Often called Sections L and M, and they must line up.

options.text: Instructions list the clauses; evaluation factors list the prices
options.why: Clauses and prices are in other sections.

options.text: Instructions are optional; evaluation factors are secret
options.why: Evaluation factors must be stated in the solicitation.

options.text: Both are written by the offeror and then checked and approved by the contracting officer
options.why: The Government writes both.

stem: A vendor asks a question whose answer could affect every offer. What should you do?

options.text: Answer it for all offerors in writing, by amendment if the terms change
options.why: Equal treatment requires that everyone get the same information.

options.text: Answer only the vendor who asked, since the question and the answer belong to them
options.why: That gives one firm an unfair advantage.

options.text: Ignore it until the closing date passes
options.why: Unanswered material questions lead to poor offers and protests.

options.text: Answer by phone to save time, then note the call in the file
options.why: Oral, one-off answers are unfair and undocumented.

stem: Where are Government contract notices and solicitations posted?

options.text: On SAM.gov, the Governmentwide point of entry
options.why: SAM.gov Contract Opportunities is the GPE.

options.text: On the agency's public social media
options.why: Social media is not the GPE.

options.text: In PIEE Wide Area WorkFlow, the DoW portal
options.why: WAWF handles invoices and receiving reports.

options.text: In CPARS, with the past performance records
options.why: CPARS holds performance evaluations.

stem: A company's bid or no-bid decision is mainly based on:

options.text: Its fit with the business, its chance of winning, the risk and the profit
options.why: These are the seller's core planning factors.

options.text: The Government's IGCE, which tells the company the price it must beat
options.why: Offerors do not see the IGCE.

options.text: The protest deadlines and the debriefing rules
options.why: Protest timing does not drive bid decisions.

options.text: Instructions from the COR about which firms should bid
options.why: CORs do not direct offerors.

stem: A prime contractor agrees to use another company as a subcontractor if it wins. This is:

options.text: A contractor team arrangement, which is legal and common
options.why: The Government recognizes teaming as a way to offer the best combined capability.

options.text: Illegal collusion that must be reported to the Attorney General
options.why: Teaming is not collusion when disclosed and not used to restrain competition.

options.text: An organizational conflict of interest
options.why: Teaming alone does not create an OCI.

options.text: Allowed only for joint ventures approved by the SBA
options.why: Prime-subcontractor teams are a separate, common form.

stem: Why should the Government care about writing a clear, stable solicitation?

options.text: It brings more and better offers and fewer protests
options.why: Companies price risk; clarity lowers prices and disputes.

options.text: It lets the Government skip evaluation
options.why: Evaluation is still required.

options.text: It removes the need for a contract
options.why: A contract is still awarded.

options.text: It matters only for sealed bids, not for negotiated buys
options.why: Clarity matters in every method.

stem: Offers that arrive after the deadline are generally:

options.text: Not considered
options.why: Late offers are generally rejected, with narrow exceptions stated in the rules and solicitation.

options.text: Considered if they are the lowest price
options.why: Price does not cure lateness.

options.text: Always considered
options.why: Deadlines protect fairness.

options.text: Considered if they are within 24 hours
options.why: There is no 24-hour grace period.

stem: In the competency model, Plan Sales is the seller's work to:

options.text: Understand the customer's needs, size up the competition and plan its sales strategy
options.why: That is the model's definition: understand the requirement, assess the competition and organize presales work into a market strategy.

options.text: Assemble and submit the offer that answers the Government's solicitation
options.why: That is Prepare Offer, the next task, where the seller carries out its sales plan.

options.text: Negotiate final prices with the contracting officer after the competitive range is set
options.why: Negotiation belongs to the Award phase (Plan Negotiations), not to the seller's pre-award planning.

options.text: Study the Government's past evaluations so it can plan a protest in advance
options.why: Protests are disagreements in the Award phase; Plan Sales is about winning business before an offer is made.

stem: Which seller task is part of Prepare Offer?

options.text: Writing and pricing the proposal so it answers the solicitation
options.why: Prepare Offer is the seller carrying out its sales plan as it assembles an offer to win the business.

options.text: Choosing which Government markets to go after over the next year
options.why: Choosing markets is sales planning (Plan Sales), done before any one offer.

options.text: Writing the evaluation factors that go in Section M of the solicitation
options.why: Section M is written by the Government buyer, not by the seller.

options.text: Reviewing and approving the Government's independent cost estimate
options.why: The independent Government cost estimate is an internal Government document; sellers never see or approve it.
